deep.reconstruction:
There are no derivations on this page. It is a verbatim excerpt in French, copied from François Arago's Oeuvres complètes, vol. 3, pp. 500–501, as the citation at the foot of the page says. It belongs to the 'R.Naturphil' notes on the physical cause of gravitation.

The content runs as follows:
(1) Historical framing. Some critics called Newtonian attraction an 'occult quality'. Newton's followers then rejected action at a distance and explained gravity either as the pressure of an aether, densest in free space and rarefied near the planets, or as the impulsion of some fluid medium.
(2) Newton never committed himself to an impulsion mechanism. The excerpt notes 'Varignon, Fatio de Duillier, Lesage', the authors of kinetic or 'ultramundane corpuscle' theories of gravity, and the copyist skips text with 'cc' (= etc.).
(3) Key physical point. If attraction is the effect of a fluid's impulsion, it must take a finite time to cross interplanetary distances.
(4) Laplace's test. Before explaining the Moon's secular acceleration by the slow decrease of the Earth's orbital eccentricity, Laplace asked whether finite propagation of gravity could cause it. His calculation showed that gradual propagation would add to the Moon's motion a perturbation growing like the square of the elapsed time. Schematically (reconstruction mine): the longitude picks up an extra term of the form k·(n·t)²·(v/c_g), where v is an orbital velocity and c_g the speed of gravity.
(5) The bound. Take the largest such t² term that the observations allow, once the known eccentricity-driven acceleration is subtracted. This gives c_g ≥ about 5×10^7 times the speed of light.

Riemann (or whoever copied this) adds no computation, comment or formula. The page shows interest in the question of a finite propagation speed for gravitation. That interest fits Riemann's known speculations on aether-mediated gravitation and light, and his 1858 retarded-potential electrodynamics.
errors: No errors by the copyist. Historically, Laplace's figures vary by source: he gives at least 100 million times light speed in Mécanique céleste (Book X), and Arago and the Exposition du système du monde give 50 million. In any case the bound depends on a specific, aberration-like model of gravitational propagation. Later work showed that in a consistent field theory (general relativity) the velocity-dependent terms largely cancel, so the bound is model-dependent and not physically valid.

results.what: A finite propagation speed of gravity would produce a secular perturbation, quadratic in time, in the lunar motion. The observed lunar acceleration (after the eccentricity effect is removed) then bounds the speed of gravity at ≥ 5×10^7 c.
results.modern_name: Laplace's bound on the speed of gravity (aberration of gravity)
results.usually_credited_to: Pierre-Simon Laplace (1776; Mécanique céleste vol. 4, 1805), reported by Arago

results.what: Survey of impulsion/aether explanations of gravitation (Varignon, Fatio de Duillier, Le Sage)
results.modern_name: Mechanical theories of gravitation, Le Sage gravitation

deep.surprise_reason: This is a reading excerpt copied from Arago, with no original content. Riemann's interest in aether theories and in finite propagation of gravity and electric action is already well documented in his Naturphilosophie fragments.

checkable.asserts: The implied lower bound on the speed of gravity in m/s, about 1.5e16 m/s.
Under the bound, gravity would cross the Sun–Earth distance in about 1e-5 s.
A perturbation proportional to t^2 is a constant secular acceleration (2k), so it can mimic the observed lunar acceleration.

transcription_corrections: 'cc' (occurring three times) is most likely an abbreviation of 'etc.', marking where the copyist omitted text.
'Arago' at the end is underlined in the manuscript.
The circled '(40)' at the right margin is the folio number, not part of the text.
The ink differs in parts of the page (some lines are paler or in pencil), which suggests the excerpt was copied in more than one sitting. The hand should be checked against Riemann's for authorship.
